transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-06-21 15:00 PDT | Duration: 46 minutes | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Arjun (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood SE), Ellen (Sable CTO), Ravi (Sable ML), Tom (Sable Infra), Ava (Sable Product)

[00:00] Maya: hi everyone thanks for joining, we're excited to scope the POC for the conversational assistant. quick agenda: success criteria, load shape, latency SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), benchmark plan, timeline. sound good?
[00:08] Ellen: yes thanks maya, quick context - our assistant is in alpha, about 2k daily active users, spike to 6k during testing windows. primary concern is tail latency during 30% of heavy workloads.
[00:18] Ravi: our current stack is on-prem inference for some models and cloud for others, we use batching in production but we have cold-start pain, and pkv cache - i mean kv cache is sometimes warm and sometimes cold.
[00:27] Arjun: quick q on traffic - do you have seq length distribution? you mentioned short prompts vs long context - what's the 95th percentile?
[00:33] Ravi: yea, most requests are 20-50 tokens, p95 around 180 tokens when users paste diagnostics, p99 hits 600 occasionally but rare. we can provide histogram.
[00:44] Lena: thanks, that matters a lot for TTFT calculation vs TPOT.
[00:49] Tom: infra constraints: our infra team limits egress and we prefer VPC peering for the POC; also want to ensure logs don't leave our VPC.
[00:58] Maya: totally, for Private / dedicated we can do VPC peering, and for hosted we have options to limit retention. we'll include SSO/SAML and SOC2 docs in the security pack.
[01:06] Ellen: good, let's focus on latency SLOs — we need definitions so the pilot can be judged objectively.
[01:12] Arjun: ok here's how we usually frame it: TTFT = time-to-first-token, measured from request arrival at ingress to the first byte of the generated response. TPOT — we sometimes call it time-per-output-token or steady-state per-token latency — basically the slope during streaming; or expressed as throughput (tokens/sec). do folks use TPOT for per-token p99?
[01:31] Ravi: yep that's helpful, in our case first token matters for perceived snappiness in UI. but when someone pastes a long log, average throughput matters more.
[01:40] Maya: exactly. So for Sable we recommend two SLOs: 1) TTFT p95 and p99 targets for short requests (seq <= 64) to capture interactivity; 2) TPOT expressed as tokens/sec or per-token latency p95/p99 for long requests (seq 200+) and also an end-to-end p95 for full response generation time.
[01:58] Ellen: can you give examples of target numbers? what are typical industry baselines?
[02:03] Arjun: typical hosted baselines on comparable quantized models: TTFT p95 ~ 60-120ms, p99 ~ 150-250ms for small seqs when model is warm and batch sizes low. TPOT or token throughput often 30-80 tokens/sec depending on model size and GPU. for private/dedicated with optimized kernels, TTFT p95 can be sub-50ms in some configs. note these numbers vary widely.
[02:23] Maya: for the pilot we should pick pragmatic targets. recommended default SLOs for the POC: TTFT p95 <= 120ms, TTFT p99 <= 300ms for seq <= 64; For long responses (seq median 200) measure end-to-end p95 <= 2.5s and per-token p95 <= 120ms (or equivalently throughput >= ~8 tokens/sec). these are starting points we can adjust based on traces.
[02:46] Ava: two quick questions - 1) should we warm KV cache before measuring? 2) how do you handle batching affecting TTFT?
[02:53] Arjun: good callouts. Measurement plan should include both cold and warm conditions. we'll run: a) cold-start tests (service freshly deployed, empty caches) to understand worst case; b) warm-warm (after steady traffic to populate KV cache) for realistic steady state. Batching: we'll run tests at multiple effective QPS and batch windows to replicate production batching policies. we also provide a harness that replays traces to preserve inter-arrival times.
[03:16] Ravi: okay we like that. how do you compute p95 for TTFT vs end-to-end generation when some requests stream?
[03:23] Lena: for streaming requests we capture three timestamps: request arrival, first token out, last token out. TTFT uses arrival->first, end-to-end uses arrival->last. for per-token TPOT we compute slope over the streaming payload (linear regression or simple duration/num_tokens). we include p50/p95/p99 buckets.
[03:42] Tom: network noise can cause spikes - do you strip out client-side jitter?
[03:46] Arjun: yes we recommend measuring at the service ingress in our infra, not from client telemetry. for network-limited customers we can run tests inside the VPC to eliminate internet jitter and optionally run egress-limited scenarios to simulate realistic constraints.
[03:59] Maya: let's talk about workloads — Ravi you mentioned 2k DAU and spikes to 6k. what QPS should we size for the POC?
[04:06] Ravi: average concurrent requests right now ~15 qps during normal, peaks ~50 qps in test windows. but some cron jobs run batch infer at 200 qps for offline jobs; those we want routed to a different pool.
[04:17] Maya: For the POC we'll focus on interactive traffic: run benchmarks at baseline 20 QPS, 50 QPS peak, plus a stress run at 200 QPS to observe fallbacks. we'll do these across short seq (<=64) and long seq (200-600).
[04:30] Ellen: timeline — we want a 4-week pilot. week 0 setup and access, week 1 baseline tooling + dry runs, week 2 formal benchmarks, week 3 run integration tests with UI, week 4 analysis and decision. are we aligned?
[04:44] Maya: sounds reasonable. Redwood recommends a 2-week warm-up before final SLO assessment but 4-week pilot length is fine if we schedule the benchmark week in week 2 and analysis in week 3.
[04:55] Ravi: what about reproducibility — we need scripts so our SREs can run them in our env.
[04:59] Arjun: we'll share the k6 load scripts and a python harness that replays requests with sequence length and inter-arrival times. It runs in docker to be reproducible. We'll include sample config to toggle KV cache warm/cold and batch window.
[05:12] Lena: measurement plan bullets that we'll do during benchmark week:
- collect seq length histogram and percentiles
- run cold start tests (3 iterations) and report TTFT p95/p99
- run warm tests after 10 minutes of steady traffic and report TTFT and per-token metrics
- run stress tests at 200 QPS to observe throttling/fallback behavior
- capture system metrics: GPU utilization, queue lengths, batch sizes, memory/kv cache hit rate, and network egress
- provide raw traces + aggregated metrics for Sable to ingest into their observability
[05:36] Ellen: good list. how about success criteria? we need pass/fail gating for the pilot.
[05:41] Maya: propose a gating checklist: 
- Functional correctness: model outputs meet quality baselines (we'll run a small eval set)
- Latency: TTFT p95 <= 120ms and p99 <= 300ms for short seq in warm tests (allow one cold-run exception)
- Throughput: steady-state throughput >= target tokens/sec equivalent to p95 per-token latency threshold (we'll define exact number after we see traces)
- Stability: no more than 2 incidents of sustained degradation (>30s) during stress window
- Security/Compliance: VPC peering, SSO, and audit log collection validated
If three of five categories pass and latency/throughput are within 10% of targets, we consider pilot a success to move to Dedicated trial.
[06:25] Ravi: that's reasonable. one more - what's the SLA if we move to dedicated?
[06:28] Maya: Dedicated has SLA options in the contract; we'll include 99.9% uptime and latency SLOs in the SOW for dedicated if you choose reserved capacity. for POC we'll not sign SLA but we'll provide SLO reports.
[06:38] Tom: on measurement specifics - what about p99 sampling noise? p99 for TTFT can vary a lot with a few outliers. do you recommend windowing?
[06:45] Arjun: yes we typically compute rolling windows (5 minute windows) and look at daily p99 and aggregated p99 across the benchmark run. We also provide histograms so you can see if p99 is dominated by a small subset. We'll annotate events (deployments, infra restarts) and exclude known infra noise if both parties agree.
[06:59] Ava: how do you capture per-route metrics? we have different assistant routes (small assistant vs deep diagnostic).
[07:04] Lena: we tag routes and provide per-route dashboards. For the POC we'll focus on two routes: interactive-dialogue (short prompts) and diagnostic-parsing (long prompts). we'll provide per-route TTFT/TPOT p95/p99.
[07:15] Ellen: ok wrap-up — items we need: redwood sends harness, pricing, and SLO template; we (Sable) send traces and network constraints; schedule benchmark week of 6/28.
[07:25] Maya: noted. we'll also include instructions for running inside your VPC and a template for result ingestion into your prometheus/grafana.
[07:31] Ravi: quick note — please include an example of how to interpret TPOT to tokens/sec conversions in the runbook.
[07:36] Arjun: will do - we'll add conversions and a small calculator in the repo.
[07:40] Ellen: thanks all. any final q's?
[07:43] Tom: none from infra.
[07:44] Ava: none.
[07:45] Maya: great — we'll follow up by EOD with links and next steps. thanks everyone.
